Chasma Couriers

Mahlzeit

Chapter 15: Olive branch

原作者：Mahlzeit，原载于 AO3。

"—and my name's Ollie now!"

I jolt upright. My right foot shifts against the mattress and my ankle detonates—ripping through what's left of the fentanyl. I bite down on the inside of my cheek as I place myself. Overhead constellations. Cabin. Bunk.

"That is—no joke—absolutely perfect for you. I was literally sitting here thinking, like, what if he's an Archie? Or maybe a Leon? Leon's cute, right? But no. Ollie. So much better."

"Really?" Ollie's voice from the cockpit. "You think so?"

Of course he told her. The name is hours old and he's already handing it out like business cards.

"Oh, I know so, honey." Through the cockpit speakers, Kathy's voice spills at a pitch that could cut through the hull. "Ollie. See? Ollie! It just rolls off the tongue. I'm gonna be saying it all day—everyone's gonna think I've lost it."

I should go in there and supervise. Kathy is harmless, but harmless people talk to people who aren't.

But I don't move. Not yet. I'm curious what Ollie will say when he thinks I'm asleep.

"Um, Kathy?"

"Mhm?"

"Can I ask you something?"

"Anything, honey."

I hear the faint creak of the pilot's chair.

"It's just, you're very different."

"Um, hello?" A half-snort, half-giggle. "Pot calling the kettle black? Have you looked in a mirror lately, mister dark-and-fluffy?"

"I mean—"

"You're starting to sound like my girlfriends. 'You're so extra, Kathy.' Like, sorry for having a personality?"

"That's not… I meant… I've met a few people who work where you work. And they're all really different to you."

"Tell me about it." She sighs. "Honestly? Everyone here is so quiet. I walk into the break room and say good morning and it's just… nothing. Crickets. I thought maybe it was a cultural thing?"

"You don't think it's… weird?"

"What, the quiet? I mean, yeah, a little. But every office has its vibe, right?"

"Um… do you know what your company does?"

*"Yeeeah? They do a lot of things. Like, all the stuff I've seen in Mr Solen's calendar. Some off-world mining, resource things, um… this sustainability division they love to advertise. Oh! And biotech—but that's a whole separate branch, I think. *

She seems more flustered than usual.

"I mean, I mostly just handle the scheduling, so I don't really see the big picture stuff. But they sponsor this charity fun-run every quarter. I haven't done one yet but I signed up. I could dig up the induction brochure they gave me, but honestly, who needs five pages just to say 'we make money,' am I right?"

That brochure is the same glossy pitch they ship to the universe at large. But you'd think the people inside the machine would have some clue about how it all works.

"Anyway, Ollie—oooh, I just love how that sounds. Ollie. Ollie! Oh, the reason I was calling—you wanted an update on Mr Solen, right? So he's wrapping up whatever off-site thing he's been doing and he'll be back tomorrow."

"Tomorrow?"

"Yep! So if you get a call, just remember our little promise, okay? No mentioning the video calls. I've never seen your cute little face."

"I won't say anything. Promise."

"You're the best, Ollie. Okay, better hop off before Finance does another one of their audits. I swear, they've got a sixth sense for—"

"Before you go."

"Mhm?"

The cockpit is quiet. I can picture him in the pilot's chair, paws curled over the armrests, legs swinging. Thinking.

"You're too nice to work in a place like that."

A long silence. My ankle throbs.

"What does that mean?" Her voice has lost its volume. "Everyone's been so lovely to me. Mr Solen gave me this job straight out of—"

"Mr Solen is a bad man."

My shoulders tense. What the hell is he doing?

"I…" Kathy starts, then stops. She clears her throat. "You're lucky you're adorable, you know that? Because that's—no. Mr Solen's the reason I'm no longer stealing formula to keep my daughter fed. He gave me this job when I had nothing—and I mean literally nothing. Literally with a capital L." A breath. "So, yeah."

Static on the line. When did I start holding my breath?

"But… I wonder…" Ollie's slower than usual. Cautious. "What do his files say about the Spindle?"

"The… the what?"

"Actually, don't worry about it."

"Oh, hell no!" Her voice snaps taut. "You can't just drop that and expect me to pretend you didn't. Is it a project? A codename? Because I have access to his emails, and I swear—"

"Bye, Kathy."

"W-what? Don't you dare hang—"

And just like that, she's gone. The static fades to nothing. The ship falls silent except for the engines and the creak of the pilot's chair.

What game is our little spymaster playing?

"Wake up."

A paw on my shoulder. Shaking me.

"Wake up."

I groan. The cabin is dark. The constellations glow above, same as always. My ankle throbs beneath the splint. "Is it my shift already?"

"We're being tailed."

I'm upright before my brain catches up, and the ankle punishes me for it. I hiss through my teeth. Ollie is already ducking under my arm, pulling the crutch from where it leans against the bunk and pressing the crossbar into my palm.

"How long?" I ask.

"It showed up on the last few sweeps. Moving fast."

He guides me through the cockpit doorway, his shoulder braced under my arm. Everything looks normal. Everything looks fine.

The radar says otherwise.

I drop into the pilot's chair, strap myself in and pull up the sweep. Our blip sits centre screen, nameless, drifting at ten o'clock. And behind us, dead on our six, a second dot.

The sweep arm rotates. Comes back around. Still on our six.

Another rotation. The gap between the two dots has narrowed.

"It's faster than us," Ollie says. He's standing beside the chair, hood up, one paw gripping the armrest.

I run the numbers in my head. Closure rate against distance. The math isn't complicated. Just unpleasant. "Ten minutes. Give or take."

"No nebula cover." He's already looked. "Not even an asteroid cluster we could lose them in. What do we do?"

The throttles hum beneath my fingers. Calyx is full steam ahead, and whoever's behind us is still gaining. Running only delays the inevitable.

So we don't run.

I grip both throttles and guide them back. The engine note drops from a hum to near-silence. The stars in the viewport slow their drift. Calyx exhales.

"We talk it out."

I navigate to the comms screen on the main monitor and swap the output to near-field. The signal-strength bar climbs from two to four.

"And if that doesn't work?" Ollie asks.

"You came to get me for a reason, didn't you?" I point at the thin black strip above the viewport. The eye-tracker switch sits on the upper console. "Flip that on."

He reaches past me and flicks it. The soft red light winks to life.

"How confident are you on reading their firepower against ours? Once we've got sight lines."

"A threat assessment?" He flicks his hood off. "Pretty confident. As long as I can see their loadout."

Good, because these lasers fire with a delay, and very few ships are as brittle as those asteroids.

I wrap my fingers around the joystick and pull. Calyx groans through the turn, her nose sweeping across the starfield, a hundred and eighty degrees. The stars slide past the viewport. When the ship settles, we're facing the way we came. Facing whatever's coming.

The radar confirms it. The dot is no longer on our six. It's dead ahead, and closing fast.

One minute.

Ollie presses himself against the console housing, out of the viewport's line of sight. His eyes are locked on the void beyond the glass, scanning for the first glint of light.

"If only I could fire the gun," he says.

"We're not firing anything if we don't have to." I flex my fingers around the joystick grip. My thumb finds the button. Rests on it. Doesn't press. "Even if we win, we don't want to be stranded in deep space with a damaged ship." I point at the viewport. "And neither will they."

I reach for the comms panel and flick the mic to open. The green transmit light blinks on.

"Hail, inbound contact on bearing one-eight-zero relative. We are not hostile. Please acknowledge."

My voice sounds steadier than I feel. The cockpit is silent. Nothing answers but the quiet ping of the radar sweep, each rotation pulling the dot a little closer. Ollie's claws clench into the chair's armrest.

Thirty seconds.

Then the speakers crackle.

"If you didn't want trouble, you wouldn't be roaming our sector." The voice is calm enough to be dangerous. "You one of Butch's boys?"

"Negative."

"Then who you with?"

I open my mouth. Glance sideways at Ollie. He shrugs.

"Ollie. We ride with Ollie."

"Don't know an Ollie."

"Because he's not from around these parts. Didn't know this space belonged to Butch." Just two professionals sorting out a misunderstanding. "Happy to be on my way. No harm, no—"

"You leave before our say-so, and we'll send you back to Ollie in a casket."

The line goes quiet. The transmit light stays green.

Casket. Said as if our lives were worth nothing. Just another thing to shove into a box and forget about. My nails dig into the joystick. My thumb traces the edges of the fire button.

Ollie's eyes lock onto something in the viewport. I follow his gaze. Between a cluster of white pinpricks, a faded red speck has appeared—so faint it could be mistaken for a dim star. A blue smear of engine bleed streaks across the black behind it.

It grows. The red deepens. Details emerge from the void. A cruiser. Comparable size to the Calyx, maybe a touch wider, with a blunt, flat-nosed profile and hull panels that don't quite match. Above the cockpit, a weapon mount. Below it, another. Dual turrets, top and bottom.

Just like us.

A second voice buzzes through the speakers. This one's lighter, higher-pitched, someone trying to talk through a laugh. "Can't believe this—a bloody hauler! Out here!" A wheeze. "Your boss ain't sending his best, mate."

The first voice returns. "Or maybe he was bullshitting. Lost little lamb."

The cruiser is close enough now that I can make out the glow of their cockpit through the viewport. Two silhouettes behind the glass. One at centre controls. One seated off to the side.

"Oi!" The first voice sharpens. "I see those guns moving. Power them down before we blast you out of the sky."

I flinch. The eye-tracker strip glows red above me, and the turrets have been following my gaze without my permission. The pirates can see the barrels shifting.

I nod at Ollie. He flicks the eye-tracker switch off. The red light dies.

"Attaboy."

"What are you hauling, boy?" The second voice is still grinning. I can hear it. "Got something good to share?"

"Or are we gonna pick the scraps from your caved-in hull?"

I flick the mic off and turn to Ollie, dropping my voice. "What are we dealing with?"

"Not good." He speaks fast. "Salvaged cruiser, compromised hull plating, probably one-third original. But underhull ballistics." He taps a claw against the console housing. "Kinetic cannon at the bottom. Instant fire. No charge cycle. Aimed right, it could punch a hole in our viewport before we blink." He shifts his gaze upward. "But the real danger is the dual missile launcher on top. Lock-on variety. Even if we manage to disable it—and it'll be tough at that angle—they fire instantly. There'll be an incoming barrage before our lasers—"

The speakers crackle. "Silence gets me real twitchy, you know—gets the trigger finger itchy."

Their weapons use ammo. Ours need a charge cycle. In a quickdraw, we lose before our beams leave the barrel. We're not getting out of this with force.

Not yet.

I flick the mic back on. "Let's be reasonable, gents. Just took stock of the hold—plenty to share. Lead us back to the shipping lane and you can have half. Easy five-hundred credits, at least."

"And stick our ass out for you to hammer with them lasers? What do you think, Gregor?"

"I think they're dreaming."

"Think I should blast a missile up their ass instead?"

I force myself to laugh. "That's, that's a good one."

They don't laugh back.

"But I'm just a hauler," I say, still awkwardly laughing. "I mean, what are you so worried about?"

Nothing comes through the speakers at first. Then, the silhouettes in the opposing viewport lean toward each other. The barest whisper slithers into our cockpit:

"…shoot this prick already?"

Ollie flinches in my periphery. Fuck. They're serious.

"H-hold on a second." Need to change tack—to my one and only wild card. "Warning you now, that'll be the most expensive missile you've ever fired."

"What are you getting at?"

"You heard the corpo broadcasts, right?" I swallow, trying to keep my voice level. "Sixty thousand credits. Bounty on a Kestrel Ten—"

"You're full of shit."

"H-hold on, Greg." The first voice drops. Quieter. I hear a muffled exchange between them. Then: "That's a Kestrel Nine."

"Actually an eight. But no one but me can tell the difference."

Silence. More muffled exchange. I catch fragments. "*…look at the nacelles… yeah but…" *

"Shit, man." The first voice comes back. "Well, thanks for rolling out the payday—"

"Before you celebrate…" I let the words land one at a time. "They weren't kidding about it being volatile. If the hull depressurises—if so much as a seam pops—this thing will make for one hell of a light show."

"Let me guess." Gregor's voice is flatter. Harder to read. "You'll blow it up unless we turn tail. That it?"

"Don't think you two are that stupid. And I'm not about to throw my life away when the only buyers are the corpos who want it back." I lean back into the chair. "So here's my offer. I'm willing to give it back to the company and split the proceeds with you. Thirty thousand credits. For doing nothing but not pulling the trigger."

The first pirate snorts. "And the corpos are just gonna forgive you? How you gonna pull off that magic trick, huh? Turn invisible when they board?"

"They don't have my face. Just a callsign. And the previous owner of this Kestrel is as stiff as a board right now, if you catch my drift. He can be our thief. Died in the struggle." I let that settle. "So you make me an honorary crew member of your fine vessel, and a perfectly intact Calyx sails into the company's arms with your name on the cheque. Then we split the money and go our separate ways. Thirty each."

Gregor jumps in first. "Gotta be kidding. We save your ass and you get to walk away with half?"

"Or you blow me up and walk away with nothing—and the company comes for your heads next." I pause. "Easy choice, if it were me."

The silhouettes huddle, heads close. The mic picks up muffled voices, too quiet to parse. Ollie shifts on the spot beside me, gripping the sleeve of his hoodie. He knows this is a bluff, but being peddled as a good with a price tag—by me of all people—can't be pleasant to sit through. Sorry, buddy.

One of the pirates gestures sharply. The other shakes his head. Another gesture. A slow nod.

"Need to check with the boss."

"You need to call him?"

"What? No, he's off shift. Sleeping." The first silhouette turns to the second. "Greg, stay here and watch the bastard. He tries anything, call his bluff."

"Aye-aye."

The centre silhouette turns and fades from the viewport. The one on the right—Gregor—moves to the centre seat. I watch him shift and settle in.

The pilot left. The one who definitely knew how to fly. How to shoot. Gregor's a side-seat man. Maybe he knows the weapons. Maybe he knows the throttle. Or maybe he doesn't know either.

I glance at Ollie. His eyes are locked on the pirates' ship. He's thinking the same thing.

"Gregor," I say. "Mind if I ask you something?"

"We're not buds."

"Well, we… we might have been, at one point. Knew a Gregor once. Went to the same academy. Fantastic pilot—one of the best in our intake, actually. Long shot, but any chance—"

"Sorry to disappoint, pal." A dry chuckle. "*I'm ex-military." *

"We had some military guys join—"

"Radar and comms specialist."

My heart skips a beat. A man who reads screens and talks into microphones for a living. But is that enough to bet our lives on?

"Oh, well," I say, "there's still a funny coincidence there."

I point at the eye-tracker switch. Then, slowly, I hold up three fingers. Ollie's eyes go wide.

"A coincidence, is there?"

"My mum, in fact. She's ex-military too. And wouldn't you know it—radar and comms specialist."

I blink at Ollie, then lower one finger. Two remain.

"No kidding?"

"But she started as a relief pilot. Before they specialised her." I watch Ollie's paw near the switch, and I lower the second finger. One left. "Apparently was common to give recruits some pilot experience first. Rotate them through the seats. That happen with you?"

"No, no. Straight pathway for me—"

I drop the last finger. Hiss through my teeth. "Now."

"—but this girl's radar is some decomm'd navy tech we were tinkering with, and…"

Ollie flicks the switch. The red light wakes. I snap my eyes to the hull plating below their viewport—centre mass, the biggest target I can find—and press the button.

The cockpit lights flicker. Every display stutters and blinks out. The engines cough, choke, and the deck vibration drops to nothing. An electrical whine builds above and below, climbing through Calyx's bones—

"He's firing! He's fir—"

Two orange beams streak across the viewport and converge on the cruiser's midsection. The impact blooms in silence—a molten eruption punching through patchwork plating. The cruiser lurches, its attitude thrusters firing wild corrections that overcorrect.

"Go for the missiles!" Ollie's voice is sharp. He's gripping the console housing, claws sunk into the metal.

I drag my eyes upward, locking onto the launcher mounted above their cockpit. I hold the button. The lights die and our engines croak, Calyx shuddering as her power is funnelled to the turrets.

Two beams lance out—but the cruiser's still rolling from the first impact. The shots slam into the hull on either side of the launcher. Metal peels back, exposing the internal skeleton: structural ribs, arterial wiring.

But the launcher itself sits between the two wounds, untouched.

"Fuck!"

Their kinetic cannon opens up. Muzzle flashes erupt from beneath their cockpit—bright little coughs of light—but their ship is still reeling and the shots scatter wide.

I hold the button. The charging cycle begins anew. Slower this time. Calyx has less to give.

Through the speakers—chopped and crackling, breaking apart as our power fluctuates—there's panic.

"—Other trigger!" A scream, fragmented. "Fire—missiles!"

The whine is climbing. Almost there. Every muscle clenched. Eyes locked on the launcher. Vision blurring at the edges.

A flicker. Two bright sparks at the mouth of the launcher. Ignition plumes. Missiles leaving the tube.

Then the lasers fire.

Both beams hit the launcher dead centre. The housing detonates, metal and mechanism blown outward in a ring of debris.

But the missiles were already gone.

Two points of light, accelerating, growing larger in the viewport.

"BRACE!"

Ollie's scream hits me at the same time my hand moves. I jam the joystick hard right. Calyx rolls, her old bones creaking. The starfield tips. The cruiser slides left across the viewport. The missiles track, bending—

The first one streaks past our viewport.

The second one hits. The portside engine nacelle.

Calyx convulses—a seizure that spreads into my skeleton. Every joint, every bone. The shockwave converges on the weakest point it can find.

My crushed ankle.

The scream that comes out of me tears my throat. My hands lose the joystick. My vision burns out. For a full second there is nothing in the universe except my ankle and the pain.

The cockpit is red. An alarm I've never heard before blares from every speaker that still works. The viewport is spinning. Stars streak past in nauseating arcs.

Ollie is face-down on the floor. Something yellow leaks from a deep gash near his wrist, staining his sleeve. I scream his name.

He shifts, head slowly turning to look at his wounded arm. He squeezes his eyes and whimpers, the sound all but swallowed by the alarm.

I fight to steady the ship. "Get up, Ollie—please!"

With a pained grunt, he shoves himself upright with his tail and stumbles against the console, dripping yellow blood onto the buttons. His paws fly across the status screens, swiping through damage reports faster than I can read them, smearing yellow streaks that glow in the monitor light.

"F-fire in the portside engine!" His voice is back, cutting through the alarm. "Deploying foam!"

He slams a button. Somewhere behind us in the guts of the ship, a muffled hiss. The remaining starboard engine sputters. The alarm keeps screaming.

As the spin slows, the cruiser drifts back into the viewport, listing badly, a hole punched into their midsection. Their kinetic cannon is still firing—aimed nowhere near us.

I hold the fire button.

The starboard engine croaks. The power systems howl in protest as every remaining circuit is rerouted to the turrets. The status screens Ollie was reading go dark. Even the alarm cuts out.

The lasers fire. The kinetic cannon evaporates, reduced to a spray of white-hot fragments that scatter into the void.

"It's over." Ollie's voice, somewhere to my left. "They're done."

I can see flames through their viewport. Inside their cockpit. The cruiser's silhouette is wrong now, bent like a broken spine. From the speakers, through the roar of static and the dying crackle of their comms system, a voice oozes through. Chopped and sliced.

"—sur-ender. We surr—"

My fingers are shaking. My whole arm is shaking. But my thumb finds the button. Presses down. Holds.

The faint glow from Ollie's damage readouts vanish. He turns. Looks at me. At my hand on the joystick. At my thumb on the button.

Two orange beams liquefy what's left above their viewport—exposed interior, the ragged stump of the missile launcher—all of it dissolving into slag that runs down their hull. The speakers break into complete static.

I keep holding the button.

Ollie's eyes are wide, the orange reflecting the fiery glow through the viewport. "What are you doing?" He clutches his bleeding wrist. "They surrendered!"

I know they have. I heard it. But I can still see muzzle flashes aimed at our cockpit. Ollie face-down, motionless on the floor. Yellow blood oozing onto the cold metal.

And I can still hear the bastard. Saying casket.

"They've got a crew. They know about the bounty. They're witnesses."

All true. None of it the reason.

The entire ship rattles as the last vestiges of power are scraped from every system—life support, lighting, heating, everything—funnelled to the two turrets bolted above and below. The charging cycle stretches. Five seconds. Eight. Ten. Calyx shudders like she's dying.

She's giving me a chance to reconsider. I just need to move my thumb. Let go of the button. That's it.

I don't want to.

The turrets fire. Both beams breach their viewport.

A blinding flash. Pure white. It fills our cockpit and burns through my closed eyelids. I reel away. The heat stings my face for a long second before it fades.

When I look back, dots smear my vision. I blink them away, one by one, until the viewport resolves.

What's left doesn't look like a ship anymore. It drifts in silence, breaking apart so slowly it almost looks staged. The cockpit is gone—replaced by a molten wound, still glowing at the edges, open to the vacuum. The fires within are already dying, each one snuffing out as the atmosphere bleeds away through a dozen fractures in the hull. Panels peel back. A section of the port side separates, trailing wires that stretch and snap like tendons. Fragments of metal and slag tumble past our viewport, some bouncing off the glass with soft, polite taps.

A slow-motion exsanguination.

My thumb slides off the button. My hand falls from the joystick and dangles limp off the edge of the chair.

Ollie's to my left. He's wrapped his yellowed sleeve around the wound. His face has retreated into the hood, the opening pulled tight to hide everything but his snout. He's trembling.

We sit in the red emergency light, watching the wreckage come apart piece by piece. Each fragment drifts away, spreading outward into the black until there's nothing left but a hollowed-out casket that could never have been called a ship.
